issues.legal_issue: A presumption that quarry rights belong to landowners cannot arise under the land-record rule unless the relevant record of rights is before the court, and a claimant who has not otherwise proved mineral title is not entitled to a declaration of that title.
material_facts: The claimant sought a declaration of a right to quarry minerals based on the alleged ownership of the landowner from whom it leased the land.
Neither party produced the relevant records of rights, although such records had been prepared for the village.
The claimant produced a later village account, but it was not the type of record in which the relevant presumption could be invoked.
The claimant had quarried only under permits issued by the Collector and had paid the prescribed royalty; it produced no evidence proving its title to the minerals.
issues.conclusion: The presumption under Section 42(2) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 could not be invoked without the relevant record of rights being before the court. The claimant did not prove its mineral title and was not entitled to the declaration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 42(2) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 raises a presumption in favour of landowners only when a post-1871 record of rights is before the court and its contents do not expressly assign the quarry to the Government; it does not establish the contents of a record that has not been produced. The absence of the public record does not justify an adverse presumption against the Government where the claimant could obtain and produce it. A claimant seeking a declaration of title must prove that title. Section 110 of the Indian Evidence Act does not assist where the claimant's possession of the minerals arose under official permits, and applying for permits is an admission that places on the claimant the burden of proving that the applications were made under a mistake.

rule.if: declaratory_mineral_title_claim and rights_record_not_produced and permit_based_mineral_possession and no_independent_mineral_title_evidence

predicates.declaratory_mineral_title_claim: The claimant sought a declaration that it had a right to minerals based on ownership attributed to its lessor.
predicates.rights_record_not_produced: Neither party placed the relevant record of rights before the court.
predicates.permit_based_mineral_possession: The claimant's extraction of minerals took place under permits issued by a public authority.
predicates.no_independent_mineral_title_evidence: The claimant did not present evidence independently establishing its title to the minerals.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks a declaration of mineral title, the relevant rights record is absent, possession arose under official permits, and no independent title evidence is presented, the declaration is denied.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot order a permit to be granted on the basis of a later change in circumstances when the challenged refusal was justified and no fresh permit application is pending.
material_facts: The claimant's permit application was refused because the land had been included in a controlled area reserved for other purposes, and quarrying was considered undesirable in the interests of residents' health.
The claimant challenged the refusal and sought an order requiring the Collector to grant a permit.
After the refusal, the legal regime supporting the controlled-area restriction ceased to operate.
The claimant made no fresh application for a permit after that change.
issues.conclusion: The refusal was supported by relevant grounds, and the later change did not entitle the claimant to an order requiring a permit to be issued because no application was then pending before the Collector.
issues.legal_principle: A mandatory order directing an authority to grant a permit cannot issue where the application challenged in the suit was properly refused and no fresh application is pending. A subsequent change in the law or circumstances does not revive an application already refused. The Court therefore did not need to decide the broader question of the extent to which a court may direct the exercise of governmental discretion over government property. The relevant statutory context included the Delhi (Control of Buildings) Act, 1955, and its replacement by the Delhi Development Act, 1957, together with the permit framework under the Delhi Minor Mineral Rules, 1938.

rule.if: mandamus_challenge_to_refused_permit and refusal_supported_by_relevant_land_use_concern and circumstances_changed_after_refusal and no_fresh_permit_application_pending

predicates.mandamus_challenge_to_refused_permit: The claimant sought an order compelling an authority to grant a permit after its application had been refused.
predicates.refusal_supported_by_relevant_land_use_c: The authority refused the permit because quarrying conflicted with a land-use restriction intended to protect the surrounding area and its residents.
predicates.circumstances_changed_after_refusal: The legal or factual circumstances supporting the refusal changed after the authority had refused the application.
predicates.no_fresh_permit_application_pending: The claimant made no new permit application after the circumstances changed, leaving no application pending before the authority.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks an order compelling a permit after a refusal supported by a relevant land-use concern, and circumstances later change without a fresh application being pending, the order is denied.
